title: Clerkships and Gains at the University of Pennsylvania and Freiburg University
paragraphs: I was allowed to do clinical clerkships at the University of Pennsylvania in the United States for two months and at Freiburg University in Germany for one month.

The University of Pennsylvania, commonly called Penn, is in the city of Philadelphia. It has deep exchanges with Nagoya University, and many seniors have been looked after by this university. It is also the university hospital with the longest history in America, and one can see scenery with history even in the city. In March it was still snowing in Philadelphia, and I spent my days regretting that I had not brought a down jacket or the like.

In the first month I did a pediatric endocrinology clerkship at CHOP (The Children's Hospital Of Philadelphia). It is, as expected, one of the leading children's hospitals in the country. Both exterior and interior were colourful, the building was large with an atrium, the atmosphere of the hospital was very bright, and many children gathered from all over. In pediatric endocrinology, thanks to the consideration of the doctor who coordinated my clerkship, I was able to take part in everything: outpatient, inpatient and consults. In the outpatient clinic in particular, I was allowed to attend various doctors and be taught one-on-one about the case I had just seen, and I was very glad and fulfilled that they gave me assignments and literature to study. The ward was where the residents were active, and they presented the patients they were in charge of at the morning rounds every day. On my last day on the ward, I asked the attending that I really wanted to present, and I was allowed to give the morning presentation. The residents kindly cooperated, and I somehow managed to give the presentation, but compared with theirs it was a difference of heaven and earth. I will never forget that when I was feeling frustrated, a team member kindly said to me, "Konomi! Good job!" Three times a week, inpatient conferences, study sessions for fellows and residents, and research reports with invited outside doctors were held ceaselessly, and I was reminded that it is a place very hungry for new knowledge and very academic. Overall, seeing the pediatric professionals who work seriously and without compromise for the children was a very good stimulus.

In the NICU rotation in the second month, I moved hospitals and went to Pennsylvania Hospital. It is the oldest hospital in the country, and the Surgical Amphitheater (a round theater where surgery was performed in public) still remains. The reasons I chose the NICU were that, besides being interested in pediatrics, the doctors there have relatively more time to spare, that I was interested in emergency care and its management, and that I thought there might be a chance to be allowed to perform procedures. This NICU puts effort into accepting students, so it was used to dealing with students, and because the coordinating doctor was a foreigner, there was also understanding for exchange students, and I was welcomed in a very warm atmosphere. After the morning examination, there was a routine of summarising each newborn's overnight data and presenting it at rounds. When I became friendly with the doctors, perhaps because my desperation came across, they began giving me an assignment every day, and as I repeated presenting on it, my literature search ability and presentation skills improved somewhat. At first I was afraid of touching babies so delicate that I feared they might break, and I did not even know how to open an incubator, but as I examined the babies every day I came to notice their changes. I became able to understand vital signs and symptoms, and each time I attended a delivery I became able to assess the condition of the newborn, and as I got used to the clerkship, there was a mountain of things to study, and every day I thought I did not want to go back to Japan yet.

At the International House Philadelphia where I stayed, many exchange students came from all over the world, and eating and talking with the friends I made there helped me enormously mentally. A Canadian friend on the same floor was doing research on tumours in graduate school aiming for medical school, and during my study abroad he was accepted into a Canadian medical school, and we were overjoyed together. Going out together to eat sushi in celebration is a very good memory. I also talked almost daily with exchange students from France, Germany, Belgium, Kosovo, Mexico and Korea.

During my stay I was also able to meet Dr. 西崎, who is active as an Attending Doctor in the PICU at CHOP. At a time when things were not going as I wanted and I lacked confidence, he showed me around the PICU, and seeing him loved by the staff, doctors and patients around him, I was able to reconfirm what I should do. I am truly grateful that he invited me to a home party and meals and gave me a lot of advice. After that, when the American clerkship ended, I flew to Freiburg, a city in the southwest of Germany. The city is built around the cathedral and is a very beautiful place full of nature. At the Freiburg Children's Hospital I was allowed to rotate through hematology and oncology. There, doctors basically do everything from blood drawing to examination and arranging what comes next, and after the examination they are chased by phone calls and paperwork, and I found differences from America and similarities with Japan. In particular, from Professor Johann and Dr. Anna, who were especially kind, I was taught outpatient examination from scratch, and they gradually let me do examinations and chart writing, which was a very good experience. They were interested in Japan, and chatting together while the three of us folded origami is a very good memory. The nurses were also very friendly and very kind to me. My thinking about pediatric tumours changed, and I came to want to study the field of oncology more. Thinking that I might not have had such a great many meaningful experiences if I had not met these doctors, I thought again that I must cherish encounters with people.

While I was preparing for the study abroad, an exchange student from Freiburg helped me look for housing in Germany. The local medical students she introduced to me also took care of me in every way and made many enjoyable memories with me. I cannot thank them enough.

I think I was able to make these two countries' study abroad fruitful because of the efforts of everyone at the International Exchange Office, and because the local doctors and hospital staff treated me kindly even though I was a foreigner whose language was insufficient. I myself was frantically trying to learn even one more thing, but before I knew it I was always being helped by the kindness of the people around me. It was a packed three months in which I learned the importance of having a sense of gratitude.
